summary: Describes an experimental mapping between the standard Telnet network virtual terminal ASCII character set and the input conventions of the UCSB On-Line System. It is a short technical note for sites using that system over the network.

plainLanguage.summary: Two systems used different keys for the same things. This note is a translation table so typing on one works on the other.

questions: nvt ascii to ucsb on-line system mapping
subtitle: Mapping network terminal keys to a specialized online system

tldr.problem: The UCSB On-Line System had 168 specialized keyboard keys, but the network terminal standard (NVT ASCII) supports only 128 characters, forcing users to enter long escape sequences to access OLS keys.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 570 defines a mapping using one-to-one assignments for common keys (A-Z, 0-9, punctuation, operators) and two-character escape sequences for less common ones. Modes (OPERATOR, ALPHABET) and options (SHIFT, INTERPRETLF) allow switching between interpretations.
tldr.outcome: Network users of UCSB OLS gained a more practical interface with single-key entry for frequent operations, reducing the need for custom keyboards while keeping backward compatibility.

today: RFC 570 is a technical specification from October 1973 documenting an experimental character mapping for network access to the UCSB On-Line System. It remains a historical record of early network terminal interoperability challenges.

sections.title: Bridging a Keyboard Gap
sections.content: The UCSB On-Line System (OLS) is a specialized system with a 168-key custom keyboard containing mathematical operators, function keys, and control functions not present on standard ASCII keyboards. The network terminal standard, NVT ASCII, supports only 128 characters. Previously, network users accessing OLS had to enter escape sequences like ;PRED[SP] (six characters) to specify a single OLS key. This made remote use cumbersome and slow, and many users wanted a custom OLS keyboard for their local machine, which was expensive. RFC 570 proposes a middle ground: a practical character mapping that gives network users faster access to OLS functionality without requiring specialized hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: OLS has lots of special keys that network keyboards do not have. To use them over the network, you had to type six characters for one key. This mapping makes it take one or two characters instead.

sections.title: One-to-One and Two-to-One Mappings
sections.content:
The mapping uses one-to-one assignment for the most common 80 or so OLS keys: alphanumerics (A-Z, 0-9), space, return, tab, punctuation, erase, and many operator keys. In USER (OPERATOR) mode, uppercase letters map to OLS operators, and lowercase ASCII triggers two-character sequences. In ALPHABET mode, lowercase and uppercase ASCII map directly to OLS alphabetics.

Two-to-one mapping uses the ESC character as a prefix: [ESC] followed by a character selects less common keys (shifted numerics, special operators like PRED, SORT, CONV, TEST). For example, [ESC]? selects the TEST key. If the character after ESC is alphabetic, it is interpreted in the opposite mode (e.g., [ESC]a in OPERATOR mode gives lowercase 'a', allowing users to type both operators and lowercase letters in OPERATOR mode).
sections.plainLanguage: Regular letters and numbers map directly. Special keys use ESC plus another key. Modes switch how letters are interpreted so you can type both operators and regular text without changing mode much.

sections.title: Modes and Options
sections.content: The RFC defines several options. OPERATOR/ALPHABET switches the mode for letter interpretation. SHIFT/UNSHIFT reverses uppercase and lowercase interpretation. INTERPRETLF/IGNORELF controls whether a line feed after a carriage return is treated as a separate DOWN arrow key (common with some terminals) or ignored (since regular terminals send CR-LF as a pair for carriage return). The RFC recommends using key labels on standard keyboards to help users remember the mapping and a reference card for two-key sequences. All of these options are selectable via SERVER TELNET commands, following previous UCSB telnet specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: You can switch between modes: OPERATOR mode for functions, ALPHABET mode for text. You can reverse uppercase and lowercase if your keyboard sends them oddly. You can ignore extra line feeds that some terminals send.
